stories.title: China’s three biggest airlines post heavy first-half losses as fuel shock bites
stories.summary: China's three biggest state-owned airlines posted combined first-half net losses of about 8.2 billion yuan (S$1.55 billion) due to surging jet fuel prices and disrupted international routes. Fuel costs rose 35-38 per cent, with little fuel hedging, exposing airlines to high oil price volatility amid Middle East conflict and a weak domestic market. The peak summer season was affected by an unusually strong typhoon season and weaker travel demand, leading to a projected 3.6 per cent passenger drop and continued profit pressure in 2026. HONG KONG/BEIJING – China’s three biggest state-owned airlines reported first-half losses for the seventh consecutive year, battered by surging jet fuel prices, with the outlook for the rest of 2026 clouded by a lacklustre summer season. Air China, China Eastern Airlines and China Southern Airlines posted combined first-half net losses of about 8.2 billion yuan (S$1.55 billion), having warned in July the figure could reach as high as 9 billion yuan. The losses were a sharp reversal from their combined first-quarter profit of 4.82 billion yuan, which was boosted by strong Chinese New Year demand, and sent their shares lower in mainland China and Hong Kong trading on Aug 31. Flag carrier Air China reported a net loss of 2.3 billion yuan, widening from a 1.81 billion yuan loss in August 2025. China Eastern posted a loss of 2.2 billion yuan, versus a 1.43 billion yuan loss in the same period of 2025. China Southern reported a loss of 3.7 billion yuan, compared with a loss of 1.53 billion yuan in 2025. The weak results underscored the post-pandemic fragility of China’s aviation sector, as the trio confronted what China Eastern described as a profit environment “severely undermined” by disrupted international routes and persistently elevated jet fuel prices linked to the Middle East conflict. Fuel costs at each of the carriers rose between 35 per cent and 38 per cent in the first half of 2026. Unlike many Asian and European rivals, Chinese airlines hedge little of their fuel purchases, leaving them more exposed to oil price swings.

stories.title: Hong Kong students, high-risk cases can get flu vaccines 1 week early this year
stories.summary: Hong Kong school students and other residents deemed at risk can receive their influenza vaccines one week earlier this year, after the government diversified its procurement efforts and streamlined administrative measures. Authorities also said on Monday it would aim to boost the injection rate among people aged 65 or above and those aged six months to two years, adding that they would rely on reminders from doctors during medical encounters as a prioritised measure. stories.headline: Hong Kong students, high-risk cases can get flu vaccines 1 week early this year

opening: Hong Kong school students and other residents deemed at risk can receive their influenza vaccines one week earlier this year, after the government diversified its procurement efforts and streamlined administrative measures.

Authorities also said on Monday it would aim to boost the injection rate among people aged 65 or above and those aged six months to two years, adding that they would rely on reminders from doctors during medical encounters as a prioritised measure.
